> * If the Control does have a type variation, the Control's overrides are applied to the type variation and removed from the Control itself:

Couldn't this lead to some very unexpected side effects if the variation is used somewhere else? Especially since theme changes can effect unopened scenes, so those side effects would not be directly visible?

> Couldn't this lead to some very unexpected side effects if the variation is used somewhere else?

Yes. For example if you have a type variation for the Button class for certain kinds of buttons, and you tinker with the overrides on one specific Button with this variation until you're happy with it, you can press the button and have that look applied to all Buttons with this variation.

Unless there are more unexpected side effects than I can think of, the idea here is that these *are* expected side effects, and also not really "side effects" since they're by design - you work on the theme style in one specific spot, then push those changes out to everyone using the style once you're happy with it.

I guess it makes sense for the workflow you describe. I was thinking about cases were you are adapting a certain button type to a new context. E.g. the button type needs a little tweak in some menu, but you'd like for all buttons in this menu to share the tweak. In such a case a behaviour that creates a new variation based on the previously assigned one might be better suited.

I think both the "Push Overrides to Current Variation" and "Create new Variation" should be available, when a Control already has a variation applied to it and the user has overridden something.

Sometimes I want to apply the changes I made to this variation to all the Controls that use it. And sometimes I want to create a new variation that has the base variation I was working on and the changes I made in the overrides, to use in the current Control and others later.

> I think both the "Push Overrides to Current Variation" and "Create new Variation" should be available, when a Control already has a variation applied to it and the user has overridden something.

I like this idea! I am wondering though, if this PR should just implement one or the other then, to start out. "Create New Variation" should be "Push to Current Variation" with a few extra steps, I think, so adding it should be relatively easy. Implementing just the "Push" action will provide a narrower, more specific scope that will make it easier to be merged.

> > Couldn't this lead to some very unexpected side effects if the variation is used somewhere else?
> 
> Yes. For example if you have a type variation for the Button class for certain kinds of buttons, and you tinker with the overrides on one specific Button with this variation until you're happy with it, you can press the button and have that look applied to all Buttons with this variation.
> 
> Unless there are more unexpected side effects than I can think of, the idea here is that these _are_ expected side effects, and also not really "side effects" since they're by design - you work on the theme style in one specific spot, then push those changes out to everyone using the style once you're happy with it.

If you want to change the variation just edit the variation in the theme editor. I think this button should just create a new variation from overrides, so always ask for a new name.

- What theme is the variation supposed to be created in? It works well when the Theme is directly assigned to the Control, but what if it's in a parent Control? Or the Control uses the project's default theme? Or there is no theme at all? Right now the button is always visible and active, even if accepting the variation name does nothing in the end.
- The editor should display a confirmation dialog before overriding values.

> Immediately refresh the Inspector so that it shows the new Type Variation and lack of overrides.

You can call `notify_property_list_changed()` on variation change.

Today I revamped the dialog box that appears. It now asks you which theme you want to create the variation on, with options being all the themes from the current Control up through the tree and then the project's default theme: The line edit for the variation name defaults to the control's current variation, and the status box below tells you if a) the name entered is valid, and b) whether this variation exists on the theme and will thus the operation will modify it, or if the variation doesn't exist so it will be created on the theme: I've also implemented the calling of `notify_property_list_changed()` so that the control's inspector updates instantly. I still need to figure out how exactly to do the button in the inspector that opens this window, but so far I'm pretty happy with this progress! 😄
The button now appears underneath the "Type Variation" property field 🙂
